Bethany McLean considers the line between wrongdoing and criminal fraud to be an interesting distinction, noting that just because a company ends up bankrupt doesn't mean the person running it is a criminal.

thesis: This episode uses Tesla, Wirecard, and Theranos as case studies to illustrate the limitations of stock price as a proxy for company quality and the distinction between civil wrongdoing and criminal fraud. The speaker argues that while public reporting can alter a company's trajectory, market warnings often fail to prevent fraud until it is too late.

claims.claim: The speaker is neutral on Tesla, seeing both pros and cons, and does not believe it is a fraud, using it only as an example of how stock price increases are wrongly used as proof of a company being fantastic.
claims.quote: And I think, oh, you naive idiots. It's not the way these things work. They go on. And I'm not, by the way, I'm quite neutral on Tesla. I see the pros and cons, so I'm not, I'm not saying that Tesla is a fraud. I actually don't, I don't believe that.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that people warned for years, maybe even a decade, that Wirecard was a fraud, with a public short seller and compelling pieces from the FT, but it didn't matter until it did.
claims.quote: If you think about Wirecard, people were warning for years, maybe even a decade that Wirecard was a fraud. You had a short seller being public. You had the FT. writing really compelling pieces about what was wrong at Wirecard, and it didn't matter until until it did.

claims.claim: The speaker cites Theranos as a counter example where the Wall Street Journal's reporting really did change the trajectory of that company.
